topics.title: Individual differences and the person–situation interaction

learn.hook: Two batsmen face the same last over with 12 runs needed. One goes calm and finds gaps; the other freezes. Same pitch, same bowler — so what made the difference?
points: Individual differences are the distinctiveness and variations among people in their characteristics and patterns of behaviour. Psychology studies, describes and measures these variations.
People differ in physical features and in psychological attributes such as intelligence, aptitude, interest, personality and values.

Behaviour is shaped both by the person and by the situation. Situationism is the view that situations and circumstances strongly influence how we act; the modern view stresses the interaction of person and situation.
A trait is a relatively stable and enduring characteristic (for example, being punctual or friendly) that shows up across many situations.
Because traits are fairly stable, they help us predict behaviour — but strong situations (an exam hall, a funeral) can make most people behave alike.

example.q: In a silent exam hall, both the most talkative and the quietest students in a class sit silently. What does this show about behaviour?
steps: Talkativeness is a fairly stable trait, so we expect differences between the two students.
But the exam hall is a strong situation with clear rules about silence.
So the situation, not the trait, decides behaviour here.
Outside the hall, the trait difference shows up again — behaviour comes from person × situation.
example.answer: Behaviour depends on the interaction of individual traits and situational demands; strong situations can override trait differences.

learn.reallife: IPL scouts look at how a player handles pressure — some young players shine in a packed stadium, others struggle. Selectors are reading individual differences in the same situation.

games.title: Term and meaning
pairs: Distinctive variations among people in characteristics and behaviour
View that circumstances strongly influence behaviour
Behaviour results from both the person and the context

games.title: Person or situation?
items: Individual differences include variations in psychological attributes like intelligence and personality.
Psychology studies variations in many psychological attributes, not only physical ones.
A trait is a temporary mood that changes every hour.
A trait is relatively stable and enduring; moods are short-lived states.
Strong situations can make people with different traits behave similarly.
Clear situational rules, like silence in an exam hall, can override trait differences.
According to situationism, situations have no effect on behaviour.
Situationism says situations and circumstances strongly influence behaviour.
Modern psychology views behaviour as a product of the person and the situation together.
This is the person–situation interaction view.

quiz.q: Individual differences in psychology refer to:
options: The average behaviour of a whole population
Differences only in height, weight and skin colour
Distinctiveness and variations among people in characteristics and behaviour patterns
Changes in a person's mood during one day
quiz.explain: Individual differences are the variations and distinctiveness among people in their characteristics and patterns of behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Restricts individual differences to physical features or to averages.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of a trait?
options: Meera is punctual in school, at tuition and with friends, year after year
Meera felt nervous before one speech
Meera laughed at a joke yesterday
quiz.explain: A trait is relatively stable and consistent across situations and time. Punctuality shown everywhere for years fits.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a passing state or single event with a stable trait.

quiz.q: The view that behaviour is largely shaped by situations and circumstances is called:
quiz.explain: Situationism holds that situations and circumstances strongly influence behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up situationism with trait theory, which stresses stable personal characteristics.

quiz.q: A shy student speaks confidently at a family function but stays silent in a new class. This variation is best explained by:
options: Only the student's fixed trait of shyness
Interaction between the person and the situation
quiz.explain: The same person behaves differently in different contexts, showing that behaviour depends on person and situation together.
quiz.mistake: Assumes traits alone decide behaviour in every context.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): People with very different personalities often behave alike at a solemn prayer meeting.
Reason (R): Strong situations carry clear expectations that can override individual trait differences.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true and the reason explains the assertion: the strong, rule-bound situation reduces trait-based differences.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reason is unrelated, missing the link between strong situations and uniform behaviour.

quiz.q: Why do psychologists study individual differences?
options: To prove that all people are basically identical
To understand, describe and measure how and why people vary, so behaviour can be better understood and predicted
To rank communities as better or worse
quiz.explain: Studying variations helps describe, measure and predict behaviour — for guidance, selection and support.
quiz.mistake: Sees the study as ranking groups or only as clinical diagnosis.

quiz.q: Which statement about traits is correct?
options: Traits fully determine behaviour in every situation
Traits are relatively stable, but behaviour also depends on situational demands
quiz.explain: Traits are fairly enduring, yet situations also shape what we actually do.
quiz.mistake: Swings to one extreme — either traits are unstable or they explain everything.

quiz.q: Case: Two equally skilled shooters compete at a national event. One performs better in front of a large crowd, the other better in quiet practice. This mainly shows:
options: Individual differences in how people respond to the same situation
That the crowd changed their skills
quiz.explain: Equal skill but different reactions to the same crowd shows individual differences interacting with the situation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the situation alters skill itself rather than each person's response.

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Why do two kids in the same class act so differently? Isn't it just the situation?'
teach.praise: Chirp! People carry stable traits, but situations matter too — it's the mix. I get it now!
teach.nudge: But if traits are stable, why does everyone go quiet in an exam hall?

learn.hook: A school counsellor in Pune has 40 students asking 'Which stream should I choose?' Guesswork won't do — she needs a systematic way to measure abilities and interests.
points: Assessment is the measurement of psychological attributes of individuals and their evaluation, often using multiple methods, against standards of comparison. Formal assessment is objective, standardised and organised; informal assessment varies from person to person and is more open to subjectivity.

Intelligence: the global capacity to understand the world, think rationally and use available resources effectively when faced with challenges. Aptitude: the underlying potential to acquire skills with training.

Interest: a preference for engaging in one or more specific activities. Personality: relatively enduring characteristics that make a person distinct. Values: enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.

Methods: psychological test (a standardised, objective measuring instrument), interview (conversation to gather information), case study (in-depth study of one person using many sources), observation (systematic, organised, objective recording of behaviour) and self-report (the person gives information about herself or himself).

example.q: A counsellor wants to know (a) whether Aarav has the potential to learn coding quickly, and (b) whether he actually enjoys coding. Which attributes is she assessing?
steps: Potential to acquire a skill with training = aptitude.
Preference for engaging in an activity = interest.
Both are needed: aptitude plus interest predicts success.

learn.reallife: Before campus placements, many Indian engineering colleges run aptitude tests and interviews. Companies combine a standardised test with an interview — that is assessment using multiple methods.

games.title: Attribute and definition
pairs: Global capacity to understand, think rationally and use resources
Potential to acquire skills with training
Enduring characteristics that make a person distinct
Enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour

games.title: Which assessment method?
items: In-depth study of one person using interviews, records and tests
Recording a child's play behaviour in a playground systematically
Filling a questionnaire about your own habits
Detailed history of a patient's life and development
Watching and noting how often a student volunteers in class
Rating yourself on how anxious you feel before exams

quiz.q: Formal assessment differs from informal assessment because formal assessment is:
quiz.explain: Formal assessment uses standardised, organised and objective procedures; informal assessment varies and is more subjective.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the two kinds of assessment.

quiz.q: Rohan has the potential to become a good pilot if trained. This refers to his:
quiz.explain: Aptitude is the underlying potential to acquire skills with training.
quiz.mistake: Confuses potential (aptitude) with liking (interest).

quiz.q: 'Honesty is always the right way to live' — this enduring belief is an example of:
quiz.explain: Values are enduring beliefs about an ideal mode of behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Treats a moral belief as an interest or ability.

quiz.q: Which method gives an in-depth picture of one individual using data from many sources?
quiz.explain: A case study is an in-depth study of a person's psychological attributes and history, using interviews, observation and tests.
quiz.mistake: Picks a single method instead of the integrative case study.

quiz.q: A standardised and objective instrument for measuring an individual's mental or behavioural characteristics is called a:
quiz.explain: A psychological test is a standardised and objective measuring instrument.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any informal method counts as a test.

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
options: Interest — preference for engaging in specific activities
Aptitude — enduring belief about ideal behaviour
Values — potential to learn a skill
quiz.explain: Interest is a preference for one or more specific activities. The other pairs are swapped.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up definitions of aptitude, values and interest.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Observation as a method requires systematic, organised and objective recording.
Reason (R): Casual watching without a plan gives reliable scientific data.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Scientific observation must be systematic and objective; casual unplanned watching is unreliable, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Believes any watching is scientific observation.

quiz.q: Case: A counsellor finds that Simran scores high on clerical aptitude but says she dislikes desk work. Her best prediction is that Simran:
options: Will surely succeed because aptitude alone guarantees success
May not succeed fully in a clerical job, since success needs both aptitude and interest
quiz.explain: Aptitude and interest together predict success; high aptitude with low interest may not lead to satisfaction or success.
quiz.mistake: Thinks aptitude alone guarantees success.

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: 'Aptitude, interest, intelligence — aren't these all the same thing? And how do you even measure them?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Aptitude is potential, interest is liking, and we measure them with tests, interviews and more. Super clear!
teach.nudge: Hmm, can you tell me one method a counsellor would actually use?

topics.title: What is intelligence? Binet, Spearman and Thurstone

learn.hook: Is a topper who aces maths but can't find her way in a new city 'intelligent'? Psychologists have argued about this for over a century.
points: Alfred Binet saw intelligence as the ability to judge well, understand well and reason well. David Wechsler defined it as the global and aggregate capacity to think rationally, act purposefully and deal effectively with one's environment.

Psychometric approach: intelligence is an aggregate of abilities, expressed as a single index (score) and measured by tests. The information-processing approach instead studies the processes people use in intellectual reasoning.
Binet's uni-factor (one-factor) theory: intelligence is one similar set of abilities used for solving any problem.
Charles Spearman's two-factor theory: a general factor (g) common to all mental tasks, plus specific factors (s) unique to particular abilities (for example, mathematical or musical).

Louis Thurstone's primary mental abilities: verbal comprehension, numerical abilities, spatial relations, perceptual speed, word fluency, memory and inductive reasoning — seven relatively independent abilities.

example.q: Kabir scores well on almost every school subject, but he is exceptionally good at music. Explain this using Spearman's theory.
steps: Spearman: every mental task draws on a general factor g plus a specific factor s.
Good performance across all subjects suggests high g.
Exceptional music skill suggests an additional strong specific factor for music.
example.answer: Kabir has high general intelligence (g) and a strong specific (s) factor for music.

learn.reallife: Government recruitment exams like SSC test reasoning, numerical ability and verbal ability as separate sections — very close to Thurstone's idea of separate primary abilities.

games.title: Theorist and idea
pairs: Uni-factor theory: one set of abilities for all problems
General factor g plus specific factors s
Global capacity to think rationally and act purposefully

games.title: Is it one of Thurstone's primary mental abilities?
items: Verbal comprehension
Perceptual speed
Word fluency
Inductive reasoning
Spatial relations
Musical intelligence
Emotional intelligence
Naturalistic intelligence

quiz.q: According to Binet, intelligence is the ability to:
options: Judge well, understand well and reason well
quiz.explain: Binet described intelligence in terms of good judgement, understanding and reasoning.
quiz.mistake: Equates intelligence with memory or physical skill.

quiz.q: Who defined intelligence as the global and aggregate capacity to think rationally, act purposefully and deal effectively with the environment?
quiz.explain: This is Wechsler's definition.
quiz.mistake: Attributes the definition to a factor theorist.

quiz.q: The psychometric approach to intelligence treats intelligence as:
options: A set of processes studied only through brain scans
An aggregate of abilities expressed as a single index and measured by tests
quiz.explain: The psychometric approach measures intelligence with tests and expresses it as a score.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the psychometric approach with the information-processing approach.

quiz.q: In Spearman's two-factor theory, 's' stands for:
options: Specific factors unique to particular abilities
quiz.explain: Spearman proposed g (general) and s (specific) factors; s factors are unique to specific abilities.
quiz.mistake: Mixes Spearman's s with successive processing from the PASS model.

quiz.q: How many primary mental abilities did Thurstone propose?
quiz.explain: Thurstone listed seven primary mental abilities.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Thurstone's seven with Gardner's eight intelligences or Guilford's 180 abilities.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of Thurstone's primary mental abilities?
quiz.explain: Interpersonal intelligence belongs to Gardner's theory, not Thurstone's list.
quiz.mistake: Mixes Gardner's intelligences into Thurstone's list.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Spearman believed that people who are good at one mental task tend to do reasonably well at others.
Reason (R): Spearman proposed a general factor g that underlies all mental tasks.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; the shared general factor g explains why performance across tasks tends to go together.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see that g is precisely what links performance across tasks.

quiz.q: Binet's theory is known as the uni-factor theory because it holds that:
options: Intelligence consists of one similar set of abilities used for solving any problem
Intelligence has three parts: analytical, creative and practical
Only one person in a family is intelligent
quiz.explain: Binet viewed intelligence as one general set of abilities.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Binet's theory with Gardner or Sternberg.

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Is intelligence one big thing or many small things? Spearman and Thurstone confuse me!'
teach.praise: Yay! Spearman says one general g plus specific s; Thurstone says seven primary abilities. Got it!
teach.nudge: And what did Thurstone say instead of one general factor?

learn.hook: Memorising the periodic table is one skill; using it to predict how sodium reacts with water is another. Jensen said these are two different levels of ability.
points: Arthur Jensen proposed a hierarchical model with two levels. Level I is associative learning, where output is similar to input (for example, rote learning and memory).
Level II is cognitive competence: higher-order skills that transform the input to produce an effective output (for example, reasoning and problem-solving).

J.P. Guilford's structure-of-intellect model classifies intellectual traits along three dimensions: operations (what the person does), contents (the nature of the material) and products (the form in which information is processed).

Guilford: 6 operations (cognition, memory recording, memory retention, divergent production, convergent production, evaluation), 5 contents (visual, auditory, symbolic, semantic, behavioural) and 6 products (units, classes, relations, systems, transformations, implications).
So the model has 6 × 5 × 6 = 180 cells, each representing a distinct intellectual ability.

example.q: How many separate abilities does Guilford's model predict, and how?
steps: Operations = 6
Contents = 5
Products = 6
Abilities = 6 × 5 × 6 = 180

learn.reallife: A student cramming formulae for JEE uses Jensen's Level I; solving a new problem that combines those formulae uses Level II — that is why coaching institutes stress practice problems, not just formula sheets.

games.title: Jensen's Level I or Level II?
items: Rote learning a phone number
Recalling a list of capitals
Repeating digits in order
Solving an unfamiliar maths puzzle
Designing a plan to fix a leaking tap
Reasoning out the cause of a power cut

quiz.q: In Jensen's model, Level I abilities involve:
options: Associative learning in which output is similar to input
quiz.explain: Level I is associative learning such as rote memory; output is similar to input.
quiz.mistake: Swaps Level I and Level II.

quiz.q: Solving a new reasoning problem by transforming given information is an example of Jensen's:
quiz.explain: Level II involves higher-order skills that transform the input.
quiz.mistake: Calls any problem-solving 'associative'.

quiz.q: Guilford's structure-of-intellect model classifies abilities along which three dimensions?
quiz.explain: Guilford used operations, contents and products.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Guilford with PASS or Sternberg.

quiz.q: How many intellectual abilities does Guilford's model propose?
quiz.explain: 6 operations × 5 contents × 6 products = 180.
quiz.mistake: Uses older counts or adds instead of multiplying.
steps: Operations = 6, contents = 5, products = 6

quiz.q: In Guilford's model, 'divergent production' belongs to which dimension?
quiz.explain: Divergent production is one of the six operations — what the person does.
quiz.mistake: Thinks divergent production is a type of content.

quiz.q: Which is one of Guilford's 'contents'?
quiz.explain: Contents are visual, auditory, symbolic, semantic and behavioural. Transformations and implications are products; evaluation is an operation.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up items from the three dimensions.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Guilford's model contains 180 distinct abilities.
Reason (R): It combines 6 operations, 5 contents and 6 products, giving 6 × 5 × 6 cells.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; multiplying the three dimensions gives 180, which explains the count.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the count comes from multiplying the dimensions.

quiz.q: Which comparison is correct?
options: Spearman stressed a general factor; Guilford described many distinct abilities across three dimensions
Spearman and Guilford both proposed exactly 180 abilities
Guilford proposed only g and s
Jensen proposed seven primary mental abilities
quiz.explain: Spearman emphasised g plus s; Guilford proposed 180 abilities; Thurstone, not Jensen, proposed seven.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which theorist proposed which structure.

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: 'Rote learning and real reasoning — are those the same? And what is this 180 business?'
teach.praise: Chirp chirp! Level I copies, Level II transforms, and Guilford multiplies 6 × 5 × 6 = 180. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: What are the three dimensions Guilford multiplies?

learn.hook: A tabla maestro, a chess grandmaster and a tribal healer who knows hundreds of forest plants — are they intelligent in the same way? Howard Gardner said: different intelligences!
points: Howard Gardner proposed that intelligence is not one entity; there are distinct, relatively independent types of intelligence that interact to find solutions.

Linguistic (using language fluently — poets, writers); logical-mathematical (logical and abstract thinking, problem-solving — scientists); spatial (forming and using mental images — pilots, sailors, sculptors, architects).
Musical (sensitivity to rhythm, pitch and sound patterns — musicians); bodily-kinaesthetic (using the whole or parts of the body with skill and flexibility — athletes, dancers, actors).

Interpersonal (understanding others' motives, feelings and behaviour — counsellors, psychologists, social activists); intrapersonal (knowing one's own feelings, motives and strengths — philosophers, spiritual leaders).
Naturalistic: sensitivity to and recognition of the features of the natural world, such as plants and animals — farmers, botanists, zoologists, bird watchers.

example.q: Mira can identify over 200 bird species by their calls and loves cataloguing butterflies. Which intelligence does she show most?
steps: Classifying and recognising plants and animals is the key feature.
That matches naturalistic intelligence.
It is not musical, even though calls are sounds — she is identifying living things.

learn.reallife: Dancers in Kathak need bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence, sitar players musical intelligence, and a Kerala fisherman reading sea and sky shows naturalistic and spatial skill — Gardner's theory fits India's rich range of talents.

games.title: Person and intelligence
pairs: Philosopher reflecting on her own motives
Farmer reading soil and crop health

items.text: Sensitivity to rhythm, pitch and melody is ___ intelligence.
Abstract reasoning and solving maths problems shows ___ intelligence.
Knowing your own strengths and feelings well is ___ intelligence.
Gardner said the intelligences are relatively ___ of each other.

quiz.q: Gardner's theory proposes that intelligence:
options: Consists of distinct types that are relatively independent of each other
Is a single general factor g
Has only verbal and numerical parts
quiz.explain: Gardner proposed multiple, relatively independent intelligences.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Gardner with Spearman's g.

quiz.q: A sculptor who can rotate and manipulate shapes in her mind shows mainly:
quiz.explain: Spatial intelligence is forming, using and manipulating mental images.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any artistic work is linguistic or musical.

quiz.q: Which intelligence is most needed by a counsellor who must understand clients' feelings and motives?
quiz.explain: Interpersonal intelligence is understanding others' motives, feelings and behaviour.
quiz.mistake: Confuses interpersonal (others) with intrapersonal (self).

quiz.q: How many types of intelligence are described in Gardner's theory as taught in NCERT?
quiz.explain: Gardner's list in NCERT has eight: linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal and naturalistic.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Thurstone's seven primary abilities.

quiz.q: A spiritual leader known for deep insight into his own thoughts and emotions shows high:
quiz.explain: Intrapersonal intelligence is knowledge of one's own feelings, motives and desires.
quiz.mistake: Picks interpersonal because a leader deals with people.

quiz.q: Case: Arjun, a national-level badminton player, can adjust his footwork in a split second during a rally. Which intelligence does this best show?
quiz.explain: Using the body with skill, flexibility and fine control is bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reading the shuttle's path is the main skill and picks spatial.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): According to Gardner, a person highly gifted in music must also be highly gifted in logical-mathematical ability.
Reason (R): Gardner held that the different intelligences are relatively independent of each other.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: Gardner held that intelligences are relatively independent, so strength in one does not require strength in another. R is true.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all intelligences rise and fall together.

quiz.q: Which pairing is INCORRECT?
options: Musical — sensitivity to rhythm and pitch
quiz.explain: Understanding others' motives is interpersonal; naturalistic is sensitivity to features of the natural world.
quiz.mistake: Mixes naturalistic with interpersonal intelligence.

teach.ask: Gappu hops around: 'My cousin can't do maths but dances like a star. Is he not intelligent?'
teach.praise: Wheee! Your cousin has bodily-kinaesthetic intelligence — Gardner says there are many independent kinds. Love it!
teach.nudge: So which of Gardner's intelligences would a dancer show?

topics.title: Sternberg's triarchic theory and the PASS model

learn.hook: A chaiwala who adjusts prices for office crowds, adds a new snack before Diwali and remembers every regular's order — Sternberg would call that practical intelligence in action.
points: Robert Sternberg's triarchic theory (1985) sees intelligence as the ability to adapt, to shape and to select one's environment to achieve one's goals. It has three parts.

Componential (analytical) intelligence: analysis of information to solve problems. Its components: knowledge acquisition (learning and acquiring), meta or higher-order (planning what to do and how), and performance (actually doing it).

Experiential (creative) intelligence: using past experiences creatively to solve novel problems. Contextual (practical) intelligence: dealing with environmental demands in daily life — 'street smartness' or 'business sense'.
PASS model (J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby): intellectual activity depends on three functional units of the brain — Arousal/Attention, Simultaneous and Successive processing, and Planning.

Simultaneous processing grasps relations among concepts as a meaningful whole (as in Raven's Progressive Matrices); successive processing handles information in serial order (recalling digits, learning spellings). Planning sets and evaluates a course of action. Das and Naglieri built the Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) to measure these processes.

example.q: Riya memorises a 10-digit phone number by repeating it in order. Later she looks at a pattern puzzle and sees how all the pieces relate as a whole. Classify each using PASS.
steps: Recalling digits in a fixed order = successive processing.
Seeing relationships among parts as one meaningful pattern = simultaneous processing.
example.answer: Phone number: successive processing; pattern puzzle: simultaneous processing.

learn.reallife: Startup founders in Bengaluru often say 'business sense beats marks'. Sternberg agrees that contextual (practical) intelligence is real intelligence, even if school tests miss it.

games.title: Sternberg or PASS?
pairs: Creative use of past experience for new problems
Seeing relations among parts as a whole
Setting and evaluating a course of action

games.title: Which component of analytical intelligence?
items: Reading and learning a new formula
Gathering facts about a topic
Deciding the steps to solve the problem
Planning how to tackle the exam paper
Actually writing out the solution
Carrying out the planned steps

quiz.q: Sternberg's triarchic theory proposes which three types of intelligence?
quiz.explain: Sternberg's three are componential (analytical), experiential (creative) and contextual (practical).
quiz.mistake: Confuses Sternberg with PASS or Spearman.

quiz.q: A student plans how she will approach a difficult problem before starting. Which component of componential intelligence is this?
quiz.explain: Planning what to do and how to do it is the meta (higher-order) component.
quiz.mistake: Thinks planning belongs to performance.

quiz.q: 'Street smartness' or 'business sense' corresponds to Sternberg's:
quiz.explain: Contextual intelligence deals with environmental demands in everyday life.
quiz.mistake: Thinks business sense is creative intelligence.

quiz.q: Using past experience creatively to solve a brand-new problem reflects:
quiz.explain: Experiential (creative) intelligence uses past experiences creatively for novel problems.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes creativity for practical adaptation.

quiz.q: The PASS model was developed by:
options: J.P. Das, Jack Naglieri and John Kirby
quiz.explain: Das, Naglieri and Kirby proposed the PASS model.
quiz.mistake: Assigns the model to theorists of other topics.

quiz.q: Learning the spelling of 'psychology' letter by letter in order uses:
quiz.explain: Successive processing handles information serially, one item after another.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any memory task is simultaneous.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Planning is described as an essential feature of intelligence in the PASS model.
Reason (R): Planning lets a person decide a course of action, carry it out and evaluate its effectiveness.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; planning's role in setting, executing and checking actions is why it is considered essential.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reason describes something other than planning.

quiz.q: The Cognitive Assessment System (CAS) was designed to measure:
options: The PASS processes of planning, attention-arousal, simultaneous and successive processing
quiz.explain: Das and Naglieri developed CAS as a battery of verbal and non-verbal tasks to assess PASS processes.
quiz.mistake: Links CAS to Gardner or personality measures.

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'Sternberg has three parts and PASS has... P-A-S-S? Help me sort them out!'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Analytical, creative, practical — and Planning, Attention, Simultaneous, Successive. Sorted!
teach.nudge: Which of Sternberg's types would a clever shopkeeper show?

topics.title: Mental age, IQ and the normal curve

learn.hook: A 10-year-old solves puzzles that most 12-year-olds solve. Is she 'two years ahead'? Binet's idea of mental age turned that hunch into a number.
points: Binet and Simon built the first intelligence test (1905). Mental age (MA) is a measure of a person's intellectual functioning relative to people of the same age group; chronological age (CA) is biological age since birth.
William Stern introduced the intelligence quotient: IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100. When MA equals CA, IQ = 100; a bright child has MA > CA, so IQ > 100.
IQ scores in a population are normally distributed: a bell-shaped, symmetrical curve with the mean at 100. Most people score near the middle; very high and very low scores are rare.
NCERT classification: above 130 very superior; 120–130 superior; 110–119 high average; 90–109 average; 80–89 low average; 70–79 borderline; below 70 intellectually disabled.
About half the population falls in the average range (90–109). Always state units: MA and CA are in years (months can be converted, e.g. 6 months = 0.5 year).

example.q: Neha's chronological age is 10 years and her mental age is 12 years 6 months. Find her IQ and classify it.
steps: Convert MA: 12 years 6 months = 12.5 years.
125 lies in 120–130, so 'superior'.

learn.reallife: Think of IQ like a cricket strike rate: it is a ratio scaled by 100. A strike rate of 100 means a run a ball — an IQ of 100 means mental age matches chronological age.

games.title: IQ bands, lowest to highest
games.prompt: Arrange from lowest to highest IQ band
items: Intellectually disabled (below 70)
Borderline (70–79)
Low average (80–89)
Average (90–109)
High average (110–119)
Superior (120–130)

quiz.q: A child has a mental age of 12 years and a chronological age of 10 years. What is the child's IQ?
quiz.mistake: Divides CA by MA (10 ÷ 12 × 100 ≈ 83).
steps: IQ = MA/CA × 100

quiz.q: A 12-year-old has a mental age of 9 years. Her IQ is:
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio and gets 133.

quiz.q: An IQ of 75 falls in which NCERT category?
quiz.explain: 70–79 is the borderline range.
quiz.mistake: Places 75 in low average (80–89) or below 70.

quiz.q: Rahul is 8 years old and has an IQ of 125. What is his mental age?
quiz.mistake: Rearranges the formula wrongly (CA ÷ IQ × 100 = 6.4).
steps: IQ = MA/CA × 100 → MA = IQ × CA / 100

quiz.q: The formula IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100 was introduced by:
quiz.explain: Binet gave the concept of mental age; William Stern devised the IQ ratio.
quiz.mistake: Credits Binet with the IQ formula.

quiz.q: Which statement about the distribution of IQ scores is correct?
options: It is skewed with most people below 70
Every IQ value is equally common
It is a symmetrical bell-shaped normal curve with mean 100
quiz.explain: IQ scores are normally distributed around a mean of 100; extreme scores are rare.
quiz.mistake: Assumes many people are at the extremes.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A child whose mental age equals her chronological age has an IQ of 100.
Reason (R): IQ is calculated as (CA ÷ MA) × 100.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: IQ = (MA ÷ CA) × 100, not CA ÷ MA.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the IQ ratio.

quiz.q: Case: Isha (CA 10 years) has an MA of 13 years. Which statement is correct?
options: Her IQ is 77, in the borderline range
Her IQ is 130, in the very superior range
Her IQ is 130, in the superior range
Her IQ is 103, in the average range
quiz.explain: IQ = 13 ÷ 10 × 100 = 130. NCERT places 120–130 in 'superior'; 'very superior' is above 130.
quiz.mistake: Puts exactly 130 in 'very superior' instead of 'superior'.
steps: 120–130 → superior

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'My mental age is 6 and I am 5 years old. What is my IQ, and what does that number mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp! 6 ÷ 5 × 100 = 120 — I'm in the superior range! The ratio of mental to real age, times 100. Yay!
teach.nudge: Which age goes on top of the fraction — mental or chronological?

learn.hook: At both ends of the bell curve are people who need understanding and the right support — one group to build everyday skills, the other to stay challenged and motivated.
points: Intellectual disability (American Association on Mental Retardation definition): significantly below-average general intellectual functioning, together with deficits in adaptive behaviour, appearing during the developmental period (before 18 years). An IQ below 70 alone is not enough.
Adaptive behaviour is the ability to be self-reliant and to adjust to the environment — communication, self-care, social skills, daily living.

Levels: mild (IQ about 55 to 70), moderate (35–40 to 50–55), severe (20–25 to 35–40) and profound (below 20–25). People with mild disability can often learn practical skills and hold jobs; those with moderate disability can learn self-care and simple social skills with training; severe and profound levels need constant support and care.

Giftedness is exceptional general ability shown in superior performance across many areas; talent is remarkable ability in a specific field. Lewis Terman's long-term study in the 1920s followed high-IQ children to see how intelligence related to success and adjustment.

Signs of gifted children: advanced logical thinking and problem-solving, high speed of processing, superior generalisation and discrimination, originality and creative thinking, high intrinsic motivation and self-esteem, independent and non-conformist thinking, and a liking for solitary academic work. Teachers, parents and tests together help identify them.

example.q: A 9-year-old scores an IQ of 65 but takes care of himself, communicates well and manages daily tasks like his peers. Can he be classed as having intellectual disability?
steps: The definition needs two things: below-average intellect AND deficits in adaptive behaviour.
His IQ is below 70, but his adaptive behaviour is not impaired.
So the definition is not fully met.
example.answer: No — without deficits in adaptive behaviour, a low IQ score alone does not meet the definition.

learn.reallife: Programmes like special schools under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act and talent-search exams for gifted students show India trying to serve both ends of the curve.

games.title: Levels of intellectual disability
games.prompt: From least to most support needed
items: Mild
Moderate

Profound

games.title: Giftedness and disability facts
items: Intellectual disability requires deficits in adaptive behaviour, not just a low IQ.
Both below-average intellect and adaptive deficits are required.
The disability must first appear during the developmental period, before 18 years.
The definition specifies onset before age 18.
Giftedness and talent mean exactly the same thing.
Giftedness is broad exceptional ability; talent is remarkable ability in a specific field.
Gifted children often show high intrinsic motivation.
High intrinsic motivation is a listed sign of giftedness.
People with mild intellectual disability can never learn job skills.
Many with mild disability can learn practical skills and hold jobs.

quiz.q: Which combination defines intellectual disability?
options: Below-average intellectual functioning plus deficits in adaptive behaviour, appearing before 18
Only an IQ below 70 at any age
Poor marks in one school subject
Slow running speed and low IQ
quiz.explain: The definition requires subaverage intellect, adaptive deficits and onset in the developmental period.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an IQ score alone defines intellectual disability.

quiz.q: Adaptive behaviour refers to:
options: The ability to change one's IQ
A person's ability to be self-reliant and adjust to the environment
quiz.explain: Adaptive behaviour covers self-care, communication, social and daily living skills.
quiz.mistake: Confuses adaptive behaviour with test performance.

quiz.q: An IQ in the range of about 35–40 to 50–55 corresponds to:
quiz.explain: Moderate: about 35–40 to 50–55. Mild is about 55–70; severe is 20–25 to 35–40.
quiz.mistake: Shifts the bands by one level.

quiz.q: People at which level of intellectual disability usually need constant care and support?
quiz.explain: Severe and profound levels involve the greatest need for continuous support.
quiz.mistake: Thinks mild disability needs constant care.

quiz.q: Giftedness differs from talent because giftedness is:
options: Skill in exactly one narrow field
Exceptional general ability shown across many areas
quiz.explain: Giftedness is broad; talent is remarkable ability in a specific field.
quiz.mistake: Treats giftedness and talent as synonyms.

quiz.q: Which is a recognised sign of a gifted child?
quiz.explain: Gifted children often think independently and are intrinsically motivated with fast processing.
quiz.mistake: Assumes gifted children need external rewards.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person with IQ 60 who shows no deficit in adaptive behaviour does not meet the definition of intellectual disability.
Reason (R): The definition of intellectual disability requires deficits in adaptive behaviour along with below-average intellect.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; because adaptive deficits are required, a low IQ alone is insufficient.
quiz.mistake: Believes IQ alone is the deciding criterion.

quiz.q: Lewis Terman's well-known long-term study (1920s) followed:
options: Children with high IQs to study how intelligence related to success and life adjustment
quiz.explain: Terman followed gifted, high-IQ children over many years.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Terman's study with stress or twin studies.

teach.ask: Gappu asks softly: 'If a child gets a low IQ score, does that automatically mean intellectual disability?'
teach.praise: Thank you! It needs low intellect AND adaptive difficulties, starting before 18. And every child deserves support.
teach.nudge: What else besides the IQ score must be checked?

topics.title: Culture and intelligence: technological vs integral

learn.hook: In some cultures the 'smartest' person finishes a task fastest. In others, the smartest is the one who keeps the family and village in harmony. Who's right?
points: Culture shapes what counts as intelligent behaviour. Sternberg's contextual intelligence implies intelligence is partly a product of culture, and Vygotsky held that cultures provide the tools for thinking.

Technological intelligence (individualistic, Western-type societies) values generalisation and abstraction, speed, minimal moves and mental manipulation — attention, observation, analysis, performance, speed and achievement orientation.
Integral intelligence (many Asian and African societies) emphasises connectivity with the social and natural environment.

The Indian notion of intelligence, buddhi (as J.P. Das describes it), includes mental effort, determined action, feelings and opinions along with cognitive competence, and knowledge of one's own self, conscience, initiative and will.

Four competencies in the Indian view: cognitive capacity (sensitivity to context, understanding, discrimination, problem-solving, effective communication); social competence (respect for social order, commitment to elders, the young and the needy, concern for others); emotional competence (self-regulation and self-monitoring of emotions, honesty, politeness, good conduct); entrepreneurial competence (commitment, persistence, patience, hard work, vigilance, goal-directed behaviour).

example.q: Classify: (a) a person who calmly controls anger and stays polite; (b) one who keeps working on a small business despite setbacks.
steps: Self-regulation of emotions and politeness = emotional competence.
Persistence, patience and goal-directed hard work = entrepreneurial competence.

learn.reallife: A self-help group of women in rural Rajasthan running a dairy cooperative shows the Indian integral idea — social harmony, patience and persistence are as 'intelligent' as speed.

games.title: Which competency in the Indian view?
items: Caring for elders and the needy
Respecting social order
Monitoring and regulating one's own emotions
Honesty and politeness
Persistence and patience in a business
Vigilance and goal-directed effort

games.title: Technological or integral?
items: Technological intelligence values speed and achievement orientation.
These are hallmarks of technological intelligence.
Integral intelligence emphasises connectivity with the social and natural environment.
This is the core of integral intelligence.
The Indian notion of buddhi is limited to cognitive competence only.
Buddhi also includes emotions, determination, self-knowledge, conscience and will.
Culture plays no role in how intelligence is defined.
Culture shapes what behaviours are seen as intelligent.

quiz.q: Which skills are typical of 'technological intelligence'?
options: Commitment to elders and the needy
Generalisation, abstraction, speed and achievement orientation
quiz.explain: Technological intelligence values abstraction, speed, analysis and achievement.
quiz.mistake: Confuses technological with integral intelligence.

quiz.q: Integral intelligence emphasises:
options: Connectivity with the social and natural environment
quiz.explain: Integral intelligence stresses relatedness with society and nature.
quiz.mistake: Picks features of technological intelligence.

quiz.q: Who described the Indian concept of 'buddhi' as including determination, will, conscience and self-knowledge along with cognition?
quiz.explain: J.P. Das described the broad Indian notion of buddhi.
quiz.mistake: Assigns it to a Western theorist.

quiz.q: 'Respect for social order and commitment to elders, the young and the needy' belongs to which competency?
quiz.explain: These are listed under social competence in the Indian view.
quiz.mistake: Confuses social with emotional competence.

quiz.q: Commitment, persistence, patience and hard work make up:
quiz.explain: These goal-directed qualities form entrepreneurial competence.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hard work is a cognitive capacity.

quiz.q: Sensitivity to context, discrimination, problem-solving and effective communication form:
quiz.explain: These are components of cognitive capacity in the Indian view.
quiz.mistake: Mixes cognitive capacity with social competence.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): What counts as intelligent behaviour can differ between cultures.
Reason (R): Gardner proposed eight relatively independent types of intelligence.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but Gardner's list of intelligences does not explain why cultures differ in what they call intelligent; ideas like contextual intelligence and integral vs technological intelligence do.
quiz.mistake: Assumes any true statement about intelligence must explain A.

quiz.q: Case: In a village, Lakshmi is called 'very wise' because she settles disputes calmly, cares for neighbours and understands everyone's needs. This view of intelligence is closest to:
quiz.explain: Valuing harmony and social connectedness reflects integral intelligence.
quiz.mistake: Assumes only speed and analysis count as intelligence.

teach.ask: Gappu ruffles his feathers: 'Is being quick at puzzles the only kind of smart? What do Indians mean by buddhi?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Western technological smarts stress speed; integral and buddhi include social, emotional and entrepreneurial skills too!
teach.nudge: Can you name one of the four competencies in the Indian view?

learn.hook: A captain who notices a teammate's shaking hands and calms him before a super over isn't using IQ — that's EQ at work.
points: The term emotional intelligence was introduced by Peter Salovey and John Mayer and popularised by Daniel Goleman (1995). It is often expressed as EQ (emotional quotient).
Salovey and Mayer: the ability to monitor one's own and others' emotions, to discriminate among them, and to use this information to guide one's thinking and actions.

Emotionally intelligent persons perceive and are sensitive to feelings; detect emotions in self and others through body language, voice and facial expressions; relate emotions to thoughts while solving problems; understand the influence of emotions' nature and intensity; and control and regulate emotions while dealing with self and others.
In short: self-awareness, managing emotions, empathy and handling relationships.
Emotional literacy programmes in schools aim to raise emotional intelligence; they are linked to better self-esteem, fewer behaviour problems and better academic and social adjustment.

example.q: Before a debate, Tara notices her heart racing, names the feeling 'nervousness', takes slow breaths and reminds herself she has prepared. Which EI features is she showing?
steps: Noticing and naming her own emotion = self-awareness.
Using breathing and self-talk to calm down = managing/regulating emotions.
Linking the emotion to a thought ('I have prepared') = relating emotions to thinking.
example.answer: Self-awareness, emotion regulation and using emotions to guide thinking.

learn.reallife: Many Indian schools now run social-emotional learning periods, such as Delhi government schools' Happiness Curriculum, which includes mindfulness and reflection — an example of an emotional literacy programme.

games.title: EI in action
pairs: Naming your own feeling of jealousy
Calming down before replying to an angry message
Feeling what a friend feels after a loss
Resolving a fight between two classmates

items.text: Emotional intelligence was introduced by Salovey and ___.
The idea was popularised by Daniel ___.
Emotional intelligence is often expressed as ___.

quiz.q: Who first introduced the concept of emotional intelligence?
quiz.explain: Salovey and Mayer introduced it; Goleman popularised it.
quiz.mistake: Credits Goleman as originator rather than populariser.

quiz.q: According to Salovey and Mayer, emotional intelligence is the ability to:
options: Monitor one's own and others' emotions, discriminate among them and use this to guide thinking and action
quiz.explain: That is their definition of EI.
quiz.mistake: Thinks EI means hiding emotions.

quiz.q: Which behaviour best shows empathy?
options: Understanding and sharing a friend's feelings after she loses a match
Ignoring the friend so she can recover
Telling the friend to stop feeling sad
Laughing to lighten the mood regardless of her feelings
quiz.explain: Empathy is understanding and feeling another person's emotions from their side.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dismissing emotions is helpful.

quiz.q: Reading a person's mood from tone of voice and facial expression is part of:
options: Perceiving and detecting emotions in others
quiz.explain: Emotionally intelligent people detect emotions through body language, voice and expressions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is a cognitive processing skill unrelated to EI.

quiz.q: Emotional literacy programmes in schools are intended to:
quiz.explain: These programmes build emotional skills, linked to better self-esteem and adjustment.
quiz.mistake: Confuses EI training with IQ training.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person with a high IQ will always have a high EQ.
Reason (R): Emotional intelligence involves perceiving, understanding and regulating emotions, which is different from academic intelligence.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: high IQ does not guarantee high EQ. R is true: EI is a distinct set of emotional abilities.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all forms of intelligence go together.

quiz.q: Case: Before replying to a rude comment in a group chat, Dev waits, calms down and then answers politely. He is showing:
quiz.explain: Controlling and regulating emotions before acting is a core EI feature.
quiz.mistake: Labels healthy regulation as a defence mechanism.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of an emotionally intelligent person?
options: Relating emotions to thoughts when solving problems
Inability to notice changes in one's own feelings
quiz.explain: Emotionally intelligent people are aware of their own feelings; inability to notice them is the opposite.
quiz.mistake: Misses the 'NOT' in the question.

teach.ask: Gappu pouts: 'I got angry and pecked my friend. Is there an intelligence for feelings?'
teach.praise: Chirp! EQ means noticing my feelings, understanding others' and managing them. Sorry, friend!
teach.nudge: What could I have done with my anger before pecking?

learn.hook: Two students love aeroplanes. One also has strong mechanical reasoning and spatial skill. Who is more likely to succeed as an aircraft engineer?
points: Aptitude is a combination of characteristics indicating a person's potential to acquire some specific knowledge or skill after training.
Aptitude and interest work together: a person with high aptitude AND interest in a field is more likely to succeed in it.

Aptitude tests come in two forms: independent (specialised) aptitude tests for one area (for example, clerical or mechanical), and multiple (generalised) aptitude test batteries measuring several aptitudes.

The Differential Aptitude Tests (DAT) have eight subtests: verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations, spelling and language usage. J.M. Ojha developed an Indian adaptation.
Uses: career guidance, educational and vocational counselling, and selection for jobs or training programmes.

example.q: A student scores high on mechanical reasoning and space relations in the DAT but low on clerical speed. Which careers might a counsellor discuss first?
steps: High mechanical reasoning + space relations → skills for engineering, design, technical trades.
Low clerical speed → routine data-entry jobs may be less suited.
Check interest too, since aptitude + interest predicts success.
example.answer: Engineering or technical fields (after confirming the student's interest).

learn.reallife: Armed forces selection boards in India use aptitude batteries before training pilots; the logic is that training is costly, so it pays to find people with the potential to learn fast.

games.title: DAT subtest or not?

games.title: Aptitude basics

This is the definition of aptitude.
High aptitude alone guarantees job success.
Interest also matters; aptitude plus interest predicts success.
The DAT is a multiple aptitude test battery.
It measures eight aptitudes.

quiz.q: Aptitude is best described as:
options: The potential to acquire specific knowledge or skills after training
quiz.explain: Aptitude refers to potential that can be developed with training.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aptitude with achievement or interest.

quiz.q: The Differential Aptitude Tests consist of how many subtests?
quiz.explain: The DAT has eight subtests.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with Thurstone's seven or the 16 PF.

quiz.q: Who developed the Indian adaptation of the DAT mentioned in NCERT?
quiz.explain: J.M. Ojha adapted the DAT for Indian use.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Indian psychologists from different chapters.

quiz.q: A test that measures only clerical aptitude is an example of:
quiz.explain: Independent aptitude tests measure one specific area.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any aptitude test is a battery.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a DAT subtest?
quiz.explain: The DAT subtests are verbal, numerical, abstract reasoning, clerical speed and accuracy, mechanical reasoning, space relations, spelling and language usage.
quiz.mistake: Adds a Gardner-style intelligence to the DAT list.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A student with high aptitude for music but no interest in it may not do well as a musician.
Reason (R): Success in a field is better predicted by a combination of aptitude and interest.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true; because success depends on aptitude plus interest, lack of interest can limit success.
quiz.mistake: Thinks aptitude alone determines success.

quiz.q: The main use of aptitude tests is to:
options: Predict future performance to guide career choice and selection
quiz.explain: Aptitude tests predict how well a person can learn a skill, aiding guidance and selection.
quiz.mistake: Confuses aptitude tests with achievement or clinical tests.

quiz.q: Case: An airline wants to choose trainees who will learn to fly quickly. What should it use?
options: An aptitude test measuring relevant abilities like spatial and mechanical reasoning
A test of how much flying they already know
quiz.explain: Aptitude tests predict the potential to learn a skill with training, which is what the airline needs.
quiz.mistake: Uses an achievement test for people who have not yet been trained.

teach.ask: Gappu puzzles: 'If I haven't learned to swim yet, how can a test tell if I could become a good swimmer?'
teach.praise: Wow! Aptitude tests measure my potential to learn with training — and I need interest too. Splash!
teach.nudge: What does aptitude measure: what I know now, or what I could learn?

topics.title: Creativity and its link with intelligence

learn.hook: List as many uses of a newspaper as you can in one minute. Wrapping, fanning, kite-making, papier-mâché... That's a creativity test, and there's no single right answer.
points: Creativity is the ability to produce ideas, objects or problem solutions that are novel (new) and appropriate (useful).

Creativity varies in level (from everyday creativity to the rare genius) and in domain (writing, painting, science, business). Heredity sets limits, but environment — opportunities, encouragement, freedom and training — strongly shapes how creativity develops.

Creativity tests use open-ended questions with no single correct answer (divergent thinking); intelligence tests mostly have one right answer (convergent thinking). Divergent thinking is scored on fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (variety of categories), originality (unusual ideas) and elaboration (detail added).

Relationship: a certain level of intelligence is needed for creativity, but beyond that level, high intelligence does not ensure high creativity — so a high-IQ person may not be very creative, and the correlation between the two is modest.
Indian psychologists such as Baqer Mehdi and Passi, along with Torrance and Guilford, developed creativity tests.

example.q: In 2 minutes, Ishaan lists 12 uses of a brick, covering building, weights, doorstops, art and garden borders, including 'grind into red powder for a Holi rangoli'. Which scores are high?
steps: Many ideas (12) → fluency.
Several different categories (building, weights, art, garden) → flexibility.
An unusual idea (rangoli powder) → originality.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on a famously small budget by finding novel and appropriate engineering solutions — creativity is not only for artists.

games.title: Creativity test or intelligence test item?
items: List all possible uses of a plastic bottle
Imagine what would happen if humans had no need to sleep
Suggest titles for a story
What is 15% of 200?
Which word is the odd one out: apple, mango, carrot, banana?
Complete the number series 2, 4, 8, 16, ...

quiz.q: Creativity is the ability to produce ideas or products that are:
quiz.explain: Creative output must be new and also useful or appropriate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks novelty alone is enough.

quiz.q: Creativity tests mainly assess:
options: Convergent thinking with one correct answer
quiz.explain: Creativity tests are open-ended and assess divergent thinking.
quiz.mistake: Confuses creativity tests with intelligence tests.

quiz.q: In divergent thinking, 'flexibility' refers to:
options: The variety of different categories or kinds of ideas
quiz.explain: Flexibility is variety; fluency is number; originality is unusualness; elaboration is detail.
quiz.mistake: Confuses flexibility with fluency.

quiz.q: A student gives 20 uses of a spoon, but all are about eating. She scores high on:
quiz.explain: Many ideas = high fluency; all in one category = low flexibility.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up number of ideas with variety of ideas.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A person with a very high IQ is always highly creative.
Reason (R): Beyond a certain level of intelligence, intelligence and creativity are only modestly related.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: high intelligence does not guarantee creativity. R is true: beyond a threshold the two are only modestly related.
quiz.mistake: Assumes intelligence and creativity always go together.

quiz.q: Which statement about the origins of creativity is correct?
options: Heredity sets limits, but environment and opportunities strongly influence its development
Creativity is fully fixed at birth
Only training matters; heredity plays no role
quiz.explain: Both heredity and environment contribute; encouragement, freedom and opportunities matter greatly.
quiz.mistake: Takes an all-heredity or all-environment position.

quiz.q: Which of these shows creativity in the domain of science rather than art?
options: Painting a new style of mural
Designing a low-cost water purifier from local materials
quiz.explain: Creativity varies by domain; a novel useful invention is scientific/technical creativity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks creativity belongs only to the arts.

quiz.q: How does an intelligence test item usually differ from a creativity test item?
options: It has one correct answer, while a creativity item allows many answers
quiz.explain: Intelligence tests are largely convergent; creativity tests are divergent.
quiz.mistake: Reverses convergent and divergent thinking.

teach.ask: Gappu flaps excitedly: 'I thought of 10 ways to use a feather! Am I creative or just intelligent?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Creativity means new AND useful ideas — and many varied ideas show divergent thinking. Feather power!
teach.nudge: Is a new idea creative even if it is completely useless?
